true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Spawned flusher processes are never killed on hang/crash restart

Processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, whose SpawnProcess class is not an instance of multiprocessing.Process (both derive from BaseProcess). The isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) check at line 254 therefore always fails for the real (non-test) processes, so a hung process is never kill()ed before _create_process_for_shards starts a replacement for the same shards. Two flushers then concurrently call flush_segments/done_flush_segments on the same Redis shards, racing to produce the same segments to buffered-segments (duplicates) or expiring each other's work. The same broken isinstance check at line 346-347 means join() also never terminate()s a hung spawned process. Use multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess (or check for threading.Thread inversely) for these checks.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

false_positives.candidate:
--flusher-processes accepts values that crash or are silently ignored

The new click option accepts any int with no validation. Passing a negative value flows through ProcessSpansStrategyFactory into SpanFlusher where max_processes stays negative, num_processes = min(negative, len(shards)) is negative, process_to_shards_map is empty, and 'i % self.num_processes' then raises KeyError/ZeroDivision-style failure while assigning shards, crashing consumer startup. Passing 0 is silently converted by 'max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)' in SpanFlusher.__init__ (line 51) into one process per shard, i.e. the opposite of what the operator requested and a surprising resource jump. Validate the option to be >= 1 (e.g. in the CLI option or SpanFlusher.__init__).

Redis memory backpressure double-counts clusters shared across flusher processes

submit() sums get_memory_info() over one SpansBuffer per flusher process (lines 298-303). Multiple shard buffers that map to the same Redis cluster each report that cluster's memory, so a cluster shared by shards in different processes is counted multiple times in both 'used' and 'available', while a cluster contained in a single process is counted once. Previously a single SpansBuffer covering all shards could deduplicate by cluster. The weighted used/available ratio is therefore skewed toward whichever cluster happens to be split across more processes, causing the hard backpressure (MessageRejected / pausing the consumer) to trigger too early or too late depending on shard-to-process assignment. Deduplicate memory infos by cluster/service before summing.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Any submit-time exception is swallowed and the offset is marked processed

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() wraps decoding, grouping and queue submission in one try/except; on any exception it logs, then add_offset()+complete_offset() for that message. If grouping_fn raises, the queue is already shut down, or queue.put() fails, the message was never processed yet becomes committable, advancing the offset and dropping the result with no DLQ/InvalidMessage propagation to Arroyo. Only genuinely undecodable/filtered messages should be skipped this way; processing/submission failures must not be marked complete.

Failed work items are marked complete and their offsets are committed

OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches every Exception from result_processor, logs it, and then unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in the finally block. The commit loop therefore treats a crashed/failed result as successfully processed and advances the Kafka offset past it, so the message is never redelivered or sent to a DLQ. This contradicts the strategy docstring claim 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and causes permanent data loss for transient processing failures.

Graceful shutdown discards queued items instead of draining them

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker.run() checks `while not self.shutdown` before each get(), so a worker that finishes its current item exits even if its queue still contains pending items, despite immediate=False intending a drain. Those unprocessed items are simply abandoned on strategy close (they will only be recovered by Kafka redelivery, if ever), contradicting the graceful-shutdown contract and delaying/losing in-flight processing on every deploy or rebalance.

OffsetTracker state is never reset when partitions are revoked or reassigned

OffsetTracker keeps last_committed/all_offsets/outstanding per Partition for the life of the factory-owned pool, and nothing clears them when Arroyo revokes a partition or reassigns it (possibly to a different committed position, or back to this consumer later at a lower offset after a group reset/rebalance). get_committable_offsets() starts scanning at max(last_committed+1, min_offset), so with a stale last_committed higher than the newly assigned offsets, no offset for that partition can ever be committed again; stale outstanding entries likewise permanently block commits. Tracker state must be (re)initialized from the partitions/offsets passed to create_with_partitions and cleaned up on revocation.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the documented guarantee

FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize, and submit() never blocks or raises MessageRejected. The strategy therefore accepts messages from Arroyo as fast as they are polled and accumulates them in memory while a slow group blocks its queue, growing memory (and the OffsetTracker's all_offsets/outstanding sets, which are only pruned up to the blocked offset) without bound and risking max.poll.interval/OOM kills. This contradicts the class docstring claims of 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up'. Bounded queues plus MessageRejected on full are needed.

Strategy close permanently shuts down the factory-owned shared queue pool

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() calls queue_pool.shutdown(), but ResultsStrategyFactory owns one FixedQueuePool and reuses it for every create_with_partitions() call. Arroyo closes the processing strategy when partitions are revoked/rebalanced and then creates a new strategy for the next assignment; the new strategy reuses a pool whose workers have exited and whose queues have been shut down. Subsequent queue.put() calls raise queue.ShutDown, which submit() then mishandles (see its exception path), so processing after any rebalance is broken and can silently drop work. The pool should be owned/refcounted by the factory, recreated per assignment, or not shut down by the per-assignment strategy.

wait_until_empty reports empty while items are still being processed

wait_until_empty()/get_stats() only sum Queue.qsize(), which counts items still waiting in the queue but not the item a worker has already dequeued and is currently processing. As soon as the last item is picked up, total_items becomes 0 and wait_until_empty returns True while processing (and its side effects) are still in flight, so callers/tests/shutdown logic relying on it can proceed or commit-check too early. Use the queue's unfinished_tasks/task_done accounting or an explicit in-flight counter instead of qsize.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key uses ambiguous underscore delimiters for name and parent

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates userUID, action, name and parent with '_' separators, but dashboard/folder UIDs legitimately contain underscores. Distinct tuples collide: (name="c_d", parent="e") and (name="c", parent="d_e") produce the identical key, as do userUIDs containing underscores combined with shifted name/parent segments. A denial for one resource can therefore incorrectly deny a different resource in a different folder for 30s. Fields should be encoded unambiguously (e.g. length-prefixed or escaped/hashed).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache blocks newly granted permissions and defeats the fresh-DB recheck

Check returns immediately on a permDenialCache hit and never re-queries the DB, while the entry written at line 154 lives for shortCacheTTL (30s) and is never invalidated when permissions change or when permCache is refreshed (e.g. by a List or another Check that fetches fresh permissions). A user who checks a dashboard/folder before its permission grant is visible, then creates/receives access to it, remains denied for up to 30s despite this PR's stated goal of letting creators immediately access newly created resources via a DB requery on cached-permission misses.

Denial cache key does not include identity type, allowing cross-identity poisoning

permDenialKey is built only from namespace, raw UserUID, action, name and parent. Anonymous subjects (anonymous:0) and the render service (render:0) both parse to UserUID "0", and user/service-account subjects can also share UID strings. A denial cached for anonymous:0 on dashboards:read/dash1 is therefore returned for render:0 on the same resource, even though getRendererPermissions would grant renderers read access to all dashboards/folders. The same collision can deny a user or service account based on another identity type's denial. The identity type (checkReq.IdentityType) must be part of the denial key.

Every cached-permission miss for a distinct resource triggers a full DB permission fetch

When cached permissions do not allow the check, Check unconditionally calls getIdentityPermissions, and this PR removed the permCache lookups inside getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions, so that call always queries basic role, teams and the permission store (singleflight only dedupes concurrent identical keys, not sequential calls). Checking many distinct resources the user legitimately cannot access (e.g. listing/probing dashboards) causes one full DB fetch per resource until each individual resource's denial entry is populated, largely negating permCache for negative checks and risking DB load under denied-request traffic.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext discards all recorded logs

TestLogger.FromContext returns a brand-new NewTestLogger() instead of the receiver (or a logger sharing the receiver's state). LoggerMiddleware.logRequest now logs via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so any test that injects a TestLogger and then asserts on that instance's InfoLogs/WarnLogs/etc. will observe zero calls because the log record was written to a throwaway instance. FromContext should return f (or a logger sharing f's Logs) so the fake remains usable for assertions.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device-limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert race

CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices in one query and then performs the INSERT ... ON CONFLICT upsert as a separate statement/session when count < deviceLimit. Concurrent requests (including from multiple Grafana instances sharing the database, where the per-instance local cache provides no coordination) can all observe count == limit-1 and all insert, exceeding the configured limit. The limit needs an atomic/serialized enforcement (transaction with locking, unique-window constraint, or serialized writer), not a check-then-act across two sessions.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Rejected device is cached as successfully tagged, bypassing the limit on retry

tagDeviceUI inserts the device ID into localCache (29-minute TTL) before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached the caller denies authentication, but the cache entry remains, so the device's next request hits the cache at line 83, TagDevice returns nil, and Anonymous.Authenticate grants an identity even though the device was never recorded and the limit is still exceeded. A rejected client only has to retry once to bypass the device limit for the cache lifetime.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Anonymous authentication now synchronously performs DB writes and loses panic isolation

Authenticate previously tagged devices in a background goroutine with a 2-minute detached-context timeout and a recover() for panics. It now calls TagDevice synchronously on the request context: a slow/count-query-backed store blocks every anonymous authentication (cache misses add a COUNT plus INSERT/UPDATE round trip), request cancellation aborts tagging, and a panic in tagging propagates into the auth path instead of being logged. This turns device bookkeeping into a latency and availability dependency of anonymous login.

New device_limit option is not declared in default/sample config or documentation

The code reads [auth.anonymous] device_limit via MustInt64(0), but this PR adds no entry to conf/defaults.ini or conf/sample.ini and no configuration documentation. Grafana convention declares every setting in defaults.ini (which also feeds config docs/overrides tooling); without it the new limit is undiscoverable for operators and omitted from generated config documentation, despite being the user-facing switch for this feature.

Provider signature changed without regenerating Wire wiring

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService changed its second dependency from anonstore.AnonStore to db.DB, and ProvideAnonDBStore gained a deviceLimit argument, but no wire_gen.go/wire set changes are included in this PR. The checked-in generated wiring still constructs and passes an *AnonDBStore where a db.DB is now expected and still calls ProvideAnonDBStore with one argument, so the server build/wire generation fails until the injector is regenerated and the now-redundant store provider binding is reconciled.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Routine cleanup batches are logged at Error level with full ID lists

Every batch in CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags logs via r.log.Error, including successful batches and empty batches, and includes the complete ids slice and SQL condition. This will emit error-level records on every cleanup cycle, polluting error monitoring, and with large batch sizes (for example the 32767 case added in tests) creates very large log lines. Routine progress should be Debug/Info and should log counts, not all IDs.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute without justification

The ticker interval is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, making all cleanup jobs, including the batched annotation cleanup, run ten times as often. This is unrelated to splitting the annotation queries and can increase sustained database load, lock contention, and the chance of overlapping long-running cleanup work (the per-run timeout is 9 minutes). The interval should remain 10 minutes unless this change is intentional and justified.

false_positives.candidate:
Parameter-limit handling only special-cases SQLite and can stall cleanup on other databases

deleteByIDs builds one bind parameter per ID for every non-SQLite database. If AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configured above the driver's parameter limit (for example SQL Server's 2100 or MySQL/PostgreSQL prepared-statement limits), the DELETE fails and untilDoneOrCancelled aborts, so cleanup cannot progress in subsequent batches. The previous subquery DELETE had no per-ID parameter limit. The delete should be chunked below the dialect's limit, or inlined/chunked safely for all supported databases, not only when SQLite's batch size exceeds 999.

SQLite ID list construction is quadratic for large batches

The SQLite branch builds the IN list with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) inside a loop, repeatedly copying the growing string. For the tested batch size of 32767 this is O(n^2) copying and can allocate substantial memory/CPU on every batch. Use strings.Builder (already imported) or strconv.AppendInt into a byte buffer to build the list in linear time.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete and DeleteCollection record metrics with wrong labels/recorder

Delete's success path calls recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, ...) passing the object name where every other call passes options.Kind, creating per-object-name time series (unbounded cardinality) and breaking kind-based aggregation. DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine at line 166 calls recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, so legacy delete-collection latency/errors are attributed to unified storage. Both misreport the metrics this PR relies on to observe async legacy writes.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete and DeleteCollection record metrics with wrong labels/recorder

Delete's success path calls recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, ...) passing the object name where every other call passes options.Kind, creating per-object-name time series (unbounded cardinality) and breaking kind-based aggregation. DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine at line 166 calls recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, so legacy delete-collection latency/errors are attributed to unified storage. Both misreport the metrics this PR relies on to observe async legacy writes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy failures are never logged

In Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection the goroutine only records a duration metric and discards the legacy error; the previous synchronous code logged legacy failures with the object context. Combined with the fire-and-forget design, a permanently failing legacy write (bad object, missing row, timeout) is invisible in logs and unrecoverable, so operators cannot detect or reconcile divergence between unified and legacy storage. Each goroutine should log the error (with kind/name) in addition to recording the metric.

Async legacy writes derive timeout context from cancelled request context

Create, Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163) start goroutines with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...) where ctx is the incoming request context. The API server cancels that context as soon as the handler returns, which happens immediately after the goroutine is spawned, so the legacy write will almost always run with an already-cancelled context and fail/be aborted. The legacy store therefore silently diverges from unified storage, defeating the stated purpose of mode 3. The goroutine needs a detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or a background context preserving values) before applying the timeout.

Legacy Create receives the pre-create object instead of the object created in unified storage

Storage.Create returns 'created', which carries server-assigned name (generateName), UID, resourceVersion and creationTimestamp, but the goroutine passes the original input 'obj' to Legacy.Create. If the storage does not mutate 'obj' in place, legacy creates a different object (different generated name/UID) or rejects it, so the two stores hold divergent copies. It also races with the caller/storage continuing to use 'obj' after Create returns. The legacy call should use the object returned by unified storage (as the previous synchronous implementation effectively did).

Legacy Update reuses the same UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the unified-storage result

The previous implementation wrapped objInfo so Legacy.Update received the exact object produced and stored by unified storage. The new code passes the raw objInfo to both Storage.Update and, asynchronously, Legacy.Update, so UpdatedObject is evaluated a second time against the legacy store's old object. If the legacy copy is missing or stale (the normal case while mode 3 is being rolled out, or after a failed async create), the legacy update computes from the wrong base, fails on resourceVersion, or creates/updates divergent content. It also shares objInfo with a goroutine that outlives the request. The result 'res' from Storage.Update should be wrapped (updateWrapper) and passed to legacy, as before.

Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes

TestMode3_Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection return as soon as the unified-storage call succeeds and never wait for or assert on the spawned legacy goroutine (no AssertCalled/waitgroup/synchronisation); several cases don't even register a legacy expectation. The core new behaviour of mode 3 — that legacy is written, with the right object, after unified storage — is therefore untested, and the un-awaited goroutines can also race with subsequent subtests sharing the package-level mocks/fixtures (mock.Mock is not safe for unsynchronised concurrent use). Tests should synchronise on the legacy call and assert its arguments, including that legacy failures do not fail the request.

Storage failures are recorded as legacy metrics in Create and Update

When Storage.Create fails, line 45 calls recordLegacyDuration, and when Storage.Update fails, line 129 does the same, even though legacy was never called and 'startStorage' measured the storage attempt. Storage error rates/latencies for create and update will be invisible while legacy metrics show phantom failures, misleading the dashboards used to judge dual-write health. These should call recordStorageDuration(true, ...).

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing double-checked cache lookup under the write lock

After releasing the read lock at line 43, multiple concurrent cache-miss callers can queue on the write lock. Once each caller acquires it, the code does not re-check entryPointAssetsCache, so every queued caller repeats the manifest file read (and any future CDN fetch) and overwrites the cache instead of returning the value populated by the first caller. Add a second cache check after acquiring the write lock for the non-Dev path.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
No concurrent regression test for the data-race fix

This change introduces mutex protection for the shared entryPointAssetsCache global but adds no test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently. Without a test exercised under `go test -race`, a future refactor could remove or bypass the locking and silently reintroduce the race the PR is intended to fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false and can panic on nil toggles

enableSqlExpressions computes enabled as the negation of IsEnabledGlobally, then returns false on both branches, so the feature flag is dead code and the intent is unreadable for anyone re-enabling SQL expressions later. It also dereferences h.features without a nil check: an ExpressionQueryReader constructed with nil FeatureToggles (as test and legacy callers do) will panic on a SQL query instead of returning the 'not implemented' error, turning a disabled-feature request into a server panic path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No tests cover the disabled SQL-expression behaviour and existing SQL tests are left broken

The stub DB makes TablesList, RunCommands and QueryFramesInto always return 'not implemented', and reader.go now rejects QueryTypeSQL, but the PR adds or updates no tests. Existing tests that construct SQL commands via NewSQLCommand/UnmarshalSQLCommand will now fail with sql-invalid-sql instead of exercising SQL, and nothing verifies the security-critical contract that a SQL expression is rejected even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled. The disabled paths in reader.go, sql_command.go and pkg/expr/sql should be covered (and obsolete SQL-execution tests removed or skipped) before merging a CVE fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path is not gated by the new disabled check

Only ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery checks enableSqlExpressions; UnmarshalSQLCommand (the legacy rawNode pipeline entry point) still calls NewSQLCommand unconditionally. It is only stopped indirectly because sql.TablesList now errors from the stub DB, so legacy callers get a misleading BadRequest 'error reading SQL command' rather than an explicit disabled/not-implemented error, and restoring a real DB implementation in pkg/expr/sql would silently re-enable SQL expressions through this path despite the CVE fix. Gate UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand with the same disabled check.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key can create duplicate Bleve indexes

BuildIndex no longer holds cacheMu during index creation and only locks for the final cache assignment. Two concurrent builds for the same NamespacedResource (for example, eager startup indexing racing a Search or watch-event getOrCreateIndex call, or two concurrent lazy builds for a missing key) can both call bleve.New/NewMemOnly, both run the builder, and both write the cache entry. For file-backed indexes they use the same directory, which can fail with lock/already-exists errors or interfere with each other; for all indexes the overwritten index is never closed, leaking its resources and leaving one caller with an index that is no longer the cached/searchable one. The previous whole-build lock serialized this; the finer-grained lock needs per-key deduplication or a check-and-reserve entry under the lock before building.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without acquiring cacheMu while BuildIndex now concurrently inserts into that map at line 138 after releasing most of its work from the lock. searchSupport.init calls TotalDocs after starting the watch goroutine, and later lazy builds can also run concurrently, so this can race with a map write and cause a fatal 'concurrent map iteration and map write' panic that cannot be recovered. TotalDocs should snapshot the indexes under RLock (or hold RLock while counting) before calling DocCount.

false_positives.candidate:
NewResourceServer now blocks on full index building and leaks background work on init failure

NewResourceServer synchronously calls s.Init(ctx) with the server's background-derived context, so construction now blocks until lifecycle init, full search indexing, and watcher setup finish, and callers cannot cancel or time out that work with their own context. If Init fails part-way (for example after search.init has started its WatchWriteEvents goroutine, which uses context.Background(), or after lifecycle Init), NewResourceServer returns nil and an error without calling s.Stop/s.cancel, leaving the caller no handle to stop the lifecycle backend or background goroutines. Previously lazy Init let server construction succeed and deferred this cost/failure to first use; eager init needs cleanup on failure and a cancellable startup context.

Postgres module-server regression is hidden by skipping the test

The change adds an unconditional skip for GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres with only a TODO saying the test does not work in Drone. This removes the only integration coverage for running the storage-server target without an HTTP server exactly in the configuration affected by moving unified-storage initialization into server construction, so a postgres-specific startup/init failure can merge and remain undetected. The skip should be tied to a tracked failure/issue or the underlying Drone/postgres init problem should be fixed instead of silently dropping coverage.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test cleanup removes a literal alias instead of the created IdPs

Inside the loop creating idp-alias-0..19, the cleanup is registered as testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove, using the literal string "alias" rather than the loop variable (alias/idp-alias-i). The cleanup therefore never removes the 20 created identity providers (and likewise the idp-alias-20 cleanup at line 425). Leftover enabled/public IdPs can leak into subsequent tests sharing the realm and skew login-IdP counts, making this and other cache tests order-dependent.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Update invalidation compares an organization-aware model against a raw model

registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate receives `original` from getById(), which returns createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(): its isEnabled() is false whenever the linked organization is disabled, regardless of the IdP's stored enabled flag. `updated` is the raw caller-supplied model whose isEnabled() ignores organization state. The LoginFilter.ENABLED predicate therefore measures different things on the two sides. For example, while an organization is disabled, changing a public org IdP from hideOnLogin=false to hideOnLogin=true yields predicate(original)=false (org disabled) and predicate(updated)=false (hidden), so no invalidation is registered; yet the cached getForLogin ID set was populated from the JPA delegate, which selects on stored fields only and contains this IdP. Once the organization is re-enabled, the stale cached set returns the now-hidden IdP (its per-IdP model is freshly fetched, so it appears enabled), and login-page callers that only re-check isEnabled() will display it. The invalidation decision must be made on comparable, storage-level enabled/linkOnly/hideOnLogin/brokerPublic values for both models.

getForLogin loses the delegate's result ordering

The cached IDs are collected into a Set (Collectors.toSet() at line 229/238) and the result is rebuilt by iterating a new HashSet (line 244) and returning identityProviders.stream(). Unlike the uncached path, which preserves the JPA/delegate stream order, the cached path returns IdPs in hash iteration order. IdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin has no documented unordered contract, so callers that do not explicitly sort (the contract previously returned getAllStream order) can see login IdPs in a different, unstable order once the cache is populated versus on the first, uncached call.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New order() method is abstract and breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

Adding `int order();` as an abstract interface method is a source- and binary-incompatible change for any CryptoProvider implementation outside the three implementations updated in this PR (custom providers, downstream projects, test providers). Such implementations will fail to compile or throw AbstractMethodError when loaded. It should be a default method (e.g. returning 0 or a documented neutral priority) so existing providers continue to work and can opt in to ordering.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)

Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
ES384/ES512 tests reuse a default-curve key pair and only assert a self round-trip

The constructor generates one EC key pair with no ECGenParameterSpec, i.e. the JCA default curve (normally P-256), and reuses it for ES256, ES384 and ES512. The ES384/ES512 cases therefore never produce real 48- or 66-byte R/S components and only assert asn1->RS->asn1->RS returns the same bytes, which would still pass for DER output that a JDK Signature verifier would reject. Each algorithm should use its matching curve (P-256/P-384/P-521) and the converted DER signature should be verified with Signature.verify (and vice versa) to prove interoperability.

Equal order() values silently select an arbitrary provider instead of detecting ambiguity

detectProvider now sorts by order() descending and silently takes element 0, but DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200. If two of those are on the same classpath (the exact situation that previously threw 'Multiple crypto providers loaded'), the winner now depends on ServiceLoader iteration order rather than any intended priority, so an application can silently run with the non-FIPS provider in FIPS mode or vice versa. Ties at the highest order need to remain an error, or the providers need distinct, intentional order values.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission returns the all-clients sentinel instead of client ids

getClientsWithPermission iterates every resource of type Clients, including the type-level resource whose name is literally "Clients", and adds resource.getName() to the result. Callers expect the set to contain client ids (specific-client resources are named by client id), so a grant on all clients contributes the useless entry "Clients" and does not expand to the ids of clients that have no individual resource. Filtering by this set therefore misses clients covered only by an all-clients permission.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fallback to all-clients resource can throw NullPointerException

In hasPermission(ClientModel, String), when no resource exists for the specific client, the code loads the all-clients resource via getResourceTypeResource() and immediately passes it to policyStore.findByResource(server, resource) and later to new ResourcePermission(resource, ...). getResourceTypeResource() can return null (e.g. the Clients type resource is absent for a resource server created before this type existed, or was not initialized), so the permission check throws an NPE/500 instead of safely returning false.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Client-removed listener can call unsupported V2 setPermissionsEnabled when both FGAP features are enabled

The listener now runs when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (v1) is enabled, but AdminPermissions.management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is also enabled, and MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() now returns ClientPermissionsV2 whose setPermissionsEnabled(ClientModel, boolean) throws UnsupportedOperationException. With both features enabled, deleting a client fires ClientRemovedEvent and this call throws, potentially failing the client-deletion operation instead of being a no-op in V2.

getResourceName has no Clients branch

getResourceName only special-cases the Users resource type: it returns "All users" for the type resource and the username for a user resource, otherwise falling back to resource.getDisplayName(). Client resources created by this PR are named by client id and have no display name set, so representations of Clients permissions/resources will show a null/empty name instead of "All clients" or the client's clientId, unlike Users.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

false_positives.candidate:
Caution overstates that the operator will fail without rolling-updates

The added caution says that while in preview the rolling-updates feature must be enabled, otherwise the Keycloak Operator will fail. The PR itself only enables the feature in UpgradeTest when an explicit update strategy is set, and the same section documents the default '<not set>' strategy as supported/mimicking 26.1 behavior. As written, existing users who do not use the new update-strategy feature would read that their operator deployment will fail unless they enable a preview feature, which contradicts the documented default path; the caution should be scoped to when the update strategy / rolling-updates functionality is used.

Feature-disabled and changed exit codes are not verified for the check command

The new test covers only the metadata subcommand and asserts only the error message; it does not assert exit code 4 and does not exercise the check subcommand with rolling-updates disabled. At the same time CompatibilityResult changes RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE from 4 to 3 and reuses 4 for FEATURE_DISABLED, a scripting/operator-facing contract. Without tests asserting 4 for disabled metadata and check, and 3 for an incompatible check result, a regression that returns the wrong code (for example picocli.exit not taking effect or the two codes being swapped) would pass while breaking automation that relies on these codes.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() grants manage to admins with only view permission

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (no-arg) returns hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE), so an admin granted only the 'view' scope on all Groups passes requireManage(). GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() relies on requireManage() to create top-level groups, so a view-only FGAP admin can create groups (and any other caller of groups().requireManage()/canManage()). It should check MANAGE only, like canManage(GroupModel) does.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authorization resource IDs, not group IDs

In V2 a specific group resource's name is the group id (see hasPermission(), which looks it up with resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)), while Resource.getId() is the internal authorization-store id. getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() passes groupResource.getId() into hasPermission(), so the findByName lookup misses the specific resource and falls back to the all-groups resource, and it adds groupResource.getId() to the returned set. Callers such as UsersResource.searchForUser() and BruteForceUsersResource put that set into UserModel.GROUPS to restrict the user query to those group ids, so the query is restricted by non-group ids (returning no members) or not restricted per-group at all. It should use groupResource.getName() both for the lookup and for the returned group id.

false_positives.candidate:
Strategy close permanently shuts down the factory-owned shared queue pool

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() calls queue_pool.shutdown(), but ResultsStrategyFactory owns one FixedQueuePool and reuses it for every create_with_partitions() call. Arroyo closes the processing strategy when partitions are revoked/rebalanced and then creates a new strategy for the next assignment; the new strategy reuses a pool whose workers have exited and whose queues have been shut down. Subsequent queue.put() calls raise queue.ShutDown, which submit() then mishandles (see its exception path), so processing after any rebalance is broken and can silently drop work. The pool should be owned/refcounted by the factory, recreated per assignment, or not shut down by the per-assignment strategy.

Graceful shutdown discards queued items instead of draining them

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker.run() checks `while not self.shutdown` before each get(), so a worker that finishes its current item exits even if its queue still contains pending items, despite immediate=False intending a drain. Those unprocessed items are simply abandoned on strategy close (they will only be recovered by Kafka redelivery, if ever), contradicting the graceful-shutdown contract and delaying/losing in-flight processing on every deploy or rebalance.

Failed work items are marked complete and their offsets are committed

OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches every Exception from result_processor, logs it, and then unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in the finally block. The commit loop therefore treats a crashed/failed result as successfully processed and advances the Kafka offset past it, so the message is never redelivered or sent to a DLQ. This contradicts the strategy docstring claim 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and causes permanent data loss for transient processing failures.

Any submit-time exception is swallowed and the offset is marked processed

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() wraps decoding, grouping and queue submission in one try/except; on any exception it logs, then add_offset()+complete_offset() for that message. If grouping_fn raises, the queue is already shut down, or queue.put() fails, the message was never processed yet becomes committable, advancing the offset and dropping the result with no DLQ/InvalidMessage propagation to Arroyo. Only genuinely undecodable/filtered messages should be skipped this way; processing/submission failures must not be marked complete.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the documented guarantee

FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize, and submit() never blocks or raises MessageRejected. The strategy therefore accepts messages from Arroyo as fast as they are polled and accumulates them in memory while a slow group blocks its queue, growing memory (and the OffsetTracker's all_offsets/outstanding sets, which are only pruned up to the blocked offset) without bound and risking max.poll.interval/OOM kills. This contradicts the class docstring claims of 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up'. Bounded queues plus MessageRejected on full are needed.

OffsetTracker state is never reset when partitions are revoked or reassigned

OffsetTracker keeps last_committed/all_offsets/outstanding per Partition for the life of the factory-owned pool, and nothing clears them when Arroyo revokes a partition or reassigns it (possibly to a different committed position, or back to this consumer later at a lower offset after a group reset/rebalance). get_committable_offsets() starts scanning at max(last_committed+1, min_offset), so with a stale last_committed higher than the newly assigned offsets, no offset for that partition can ever be committed again; stale outstanding entries likewise permanently block commits. Tracker state must be (re)initialized from the partitions/offsets passed to create_with_partitions and cleaned up on revocation.

wait_until_empty reports empty while items are still being processed

wait_until_empty()/get_stats() only sum Queue.qsize(), which counts items still waiting in the queue but not the item a worker has already dequeued and is currently processing. As soon as the last item is picked up, total_items becomes 0 and wait_until_empty returns True while processing (and its side effects) are still in flight, so callers/tests/shutdown logic relying on it can proceed or commit-check too early. Use the queue's unfinished_tasks/task_done accounting or an explicit in-flight counter instead of qsize.

false_positives.candidate:
ZUNIONSTORE defaults to SUM and corrupts end_timestamp scores for duplicate spans

The migration from SUNIONSTORE to ZUNIONSTORE uses the default aggregate SUM. If the same span payload exists in both the destination and merged set (retries/re-deliveries are expected in this consumer), its score becomes the sum of the two end_timestamp_precise values (~2x a Unix timestamp) instead of the span's end time. That corrupts eviction ordering in the same script: duplicated spans look far-future and are retained while non-duplicated earlier spans are popped. The union needs an explicit aggregate such as MAX (or weights 1,0 semantics) to preserve scores.

Insert-time ZPOPMIN silently discards the earliest-ending spans from a segment

When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, this pops span_count-1000 members with the smallest end_timestamp_precise scores with no metric, log, or dropped-segment marker. Those spans are permanently lost before flushing, so downstream receives an incomplete segment indistinguishable from a complete one; depending on timestamps this can drop children that ended early while keeping later spans. The previous Python-side behavior at least counted/logged oversized segments and skipped them explicitly rather than silently emitting a truncated segment.

Removal of max_segment_spans guard lets oversized segments load unbounded at flush

_load_segment_data no longer enforces self.max_segment_spans; only the byte-size guard remains. Segments created before this deploy (plain Redis SETs are also incompatible, see zadd change), segments written by old consumers during a rolling deploy, or any path that bypasses the Lua cap can now accumulate arbitrarily many small payloads and be fully materialized into memory in payloads[key], risking consumer OOM instead of the previous counted/logged skip. The Lua hardcoded 1000 also ignores the configurable max_segment_spans=1001 setting.

Changing span sets to sorted sets breaks in-flight segments stored as Redis SETs

process_spans now issues ZADD and the Lua script issues ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZPOPMIN against span-buf:s:* keys, and _load_segment_data issues ZSCAN. Segments already buffered at deploy time are regular SETs (created by SADD/SUNIONSTORE) with a 3600s TTL; every one of these commands against them returns WRONGTYPE, failing process_spans/flush until the old keys expire and losing/delaying those in-flight segments. No migration, key versioning, or type handling is provided.

Redirect chain traversal limit cut from 10000 to 1000 without justification

The loop that follows span-buf:sr redirects to find the canonical segment set now stops after 1000 hops instead of 10000; the removed comment noted trees deeper than the limit may not be joined correctly. Deep segment trees between 1000 and 10000 redirects will be split into multiple segments (wrong segment_id/is_segment attribution downstream) — a silent correctness regression unrelated to the stated eviction optimization.

New required end_timestamp_precise lookup can poison-batch on messages lacking it

process_batch now does val['end_timestamp_precise'] unconditionally while constructing Span (and Span gained the field with no default). Any ingest-spans message missing that field — older producers, partially-formed spans, or schema variants previously accepted since only trace/span/project ids were read — raises KeyError for the whole batch, causing redelivery loops for that batch. Use a fallback (e.g. end_timestamp or message timestamp) or give Span a default.

No test covers eviction, score preservation, or the new paginator

The test changes only add the now-required end_timestamp_precise field to existing fixtures. Nothing exercises a segment exceeding 1000 spans (which spans get evicted, whether the root span survives), duplicate-payload merges preserving scores under ZUNIONSTORE, or OptimizedCursorPaginator/negative cursors. The core behavioral change of this PR — insert-time eviction — would pass CI even if it dropped the wrong spans or crashed.

However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

Missing double-checked cache lookup under the write lock

After releasing the read lock at line 43, multiple concurrent cache-miss callers can queue on the write lock. Once each caller acquires it, the code does not re-check entryPointAssetsCache, so every queued caller repeats the manifest file read (and any future CDN fetch) and overwrites the cache instead of returning the value populated by the first caller. Add a second cache check after acquiring the write lock for the non-Dev path.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same concurrency issue: an incomplete double-checked locking pattern where the cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock following a read lock miss.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive timeout context from cancelled request context

Create, Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163) start goroutines with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...) where ctx is the incoming request context. The API server cancels that context as soon as the handler returns, which happens immediately after the goroutine is spawned, so the legacy write will almost always run with an already-cancelled context and fail/be aborted. The legacy store therefore silently diverges from unified storage, defeating the stated purpose of mode 3. The goroutine needs a detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or a background context preserving values) before applying the timeout.

Legacy Create receives the pre-create object instead of the object created in unified storage

Storage.Create returns 'created', which carries server-assigned name (generateName), UID, resourceVersion and creationTimestamp, but the goroutine passes the original input 'obj' to Legacy.Create. If the storage does not mutate 'obj' in place, legacy creates a different object (different generated name/UID) or rejects it, so the two stores hold divergent copies. It also races with the caller/storage continuing to use 'obj' after Create returns. The legacy call should use the object returned by unified storage (as the previous synchronous implementation effectively did).

Legacy Update reuses the same UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the unified-storage result

The previous implementation wrapped objInfo so Legacy.Update received the exact object produced and stored by unified storage. The new code passes the raw objInfo to both Storage.Update and, asynchronously, Legacy.Update, so UpdatedObject is evaluated a second time against the legacy store's old object. If the legacy copy is missing or stale (the normal case while mode 3 is being rolled out, or after a failed async create), the legacy update computes from the wrong base, fails on resourceVersion, or creates/updates divergent content. It also shares objInfo with a goroutine that outlives the request. The result 'res' from Storage.Update should be wrapped (updateWrapper) and passed to legacy, as before.

Async legacy failures are never logged

In Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection the goroutine only records a duration metric and discards the legacy error; the previous synchronous code logged legacy failures with the object context. Combined with the fire-and-forget design, a permanently failing legacy write (bad object, missing row, timeout) is invisible in logs and unrecoverable, so operators cannot detect or reconcile divergence between unified and legacy storage. Each goroutine should log the error (with kind/name) in addition to recording the metric.

Storage failures are recorded as legacy metrics in Create and Update

When Storage.Create fails, line 45 calls recordLegacyDuration, and when Storage.Update fails, line 129 does the same, even though legacy was never called and 'startStorage' measured the storage attempt. Storage error rates/latencies for create and update will be invisible while legacy metrics show phantom failures, misleading the dashboards used to judge dual-write health. These should call recordStorageDuration(true, ...).

Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes

TestMode3_Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection return as soon as the unified-storage call succeeds and never wait for or assert on the spawned legacy goroutine (no AssertCalled/waitgroup/synchronisation); several cases don't even register a legacy expectation. The core new behaviour of mode 3 — that legacy is written, with the right object, after unified storage — is therefore untested, and the un-awaited goroutines can also race with subsequent subtests sharing the package-level mocks/fixtures (mock.Mock is not safe for unsynchronised concurrent use). Tests should synchronise on the legacy call and assert its arguments, including that legacy failures do not fail the request.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are only loaded for web requests, not jobs/mailers

I18n.translate only calls load_locale(config.locale), never the fallback locales returned by I18n.fallbacks. Fallback locales are loaded solely by ApplicationController#set_locale via I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!, so code running outside a request (Sidekiq jobs, mailers, rake tasks, console) in a non-English locale will attempt fallback lookups against locale files that were never loaded and return 'translation missing' instead of the site-default/English string, unless a web request previously happened to load them in the same process. The fix must load the fallback chain inside the translation path (or ensure_loaded! must be invoked for all execution contexts), not just in a controller before_filter.

Fallback calculation crashes if default_locale is unset and depends on DB-backed settings during translation

FallbackLocaleList#[] calls SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym on every fallback lookup. If default_locale is nil/blank (fresh install, boot/rake/migration contexts before site settings are available, or a cleared setting), this raises NoMethodError on nil (or produces the invalid locale :""), turning an otherwise recoverable missing-translation case into an exception for any I18n.t call. It also makes the low-level I18n backend depend on a database-backed SiteSetting lookup during translation, including during initialization when the settings table may not exist yet. Guard nil/blank and avoid requiring SiteSetting availability for the :en fallback.

Fallback list recomputes SiteSetting lookup on every missing translation

I18n::Backend::Fallbacks invokes I18n.fallbacks[locale] each time it retries a lookup, and this implementation allocates a new array and calls SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym (a settings-store lookup) on every invocation, with no memoization. On pages/emails with many untranslated keys in a non-English locale this adds repeated settings lookups and allocations to the hot translation path, partially defeating the translation LRU-cache accelerator. Cache the computed chain per locale (invalidating when default_locale changes) or compute the default once.

No tests cover the new fallback chain or its interaction with lazy locale loading

This PR replaces Rails' config.i18n.fallbacks with a custom FallbackLocaleList, changes the backend module inclusion (pluralization + fallbacks), deletes the old pluralization initializer, and adds a lazy ensure_loaded! path, but adds no specs. There is no coverage proving: a missing key in a user locale falls back to the site locale then :en, fallback files are actually loaded on demand, pluralization still works through the fallback locale, or behavior outside ApplicationController. Given the lazy-loading accelerator makes fallback success dependent on which locales happen to be loaded, a regression would silently surface as 'translation missing' strings in production.

false_positives.candidate:
New abstract getShortcut() breaks all custom OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations

OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is an SPI implemented by extensions outside this repository. Adding getShortcut() as an abstract interface method makes every existing custom factory fail to compile and, if deployed as an old binary, throw AbstractMethodError when Keycloak enumerates grant factories in DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit/getShortcutByGrantType. It should be a default method (e.g. returning a fallback/'na' or a derived 2-char value) so existing grants keep issuing tokens.

Public copy constructor of OAuth2GrantType.Context was removed

The PR deletes the public Context(Context) copy constructor while adding grantType extraction to the main constructor. Any grant/token-exchange code or custom extension that wrapped an existing Context via the copy constructor will no longer compile and old binaries will throw NoSuchMethodError. The copy constructor should be retained (and updated to copy grantType) or explicitly deprecated rather than removed.

Token issuance now hard-fails for unknown or custom grant types

TokenManager.initToken unconditionally calls encodeTokenId for every access token. getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext only falls back to 'na' when the GRANT_TYPE attribute is null; if the attribute holds any value not registered as an OAuth2GrantTypeFactory id (custom grants, internal/direct token creation paths that set a grant string, or grants whose factory returns no shortcut) getShortcutByGrantType returns null and encodeTokenId throws IllegalStateException, aborting token issuance entirely instead of encoding the token with the 'na' unknown marker.

Null or duplicate shortcuts put into ConcurrentHashMap cause NPE or misleading startup failure

postInit unconditionally does grantsByShortcuts.put(gtf.getShortcut(), grantName) and grantsToShortcuts.put(grantName, grantShortcut) on ConcurrentHashMaps. If any grant factory (in particular a legacy/custom one given a default getShortcut, or one returning null) returns null, ConcurrentHashMap throws NullPointerException during startup with no indication of which grant caused it. Shortcut nullness/length/uniqueness should be validated explicitly with the grant id in the error message before inserting.

RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential now prefers a federated credential, but when all its codes are used this code calls removeStoredCredentialById, which only removes a credential from Keycloak's local DB. true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New order() method is abstract and breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

Adding `int order();` as an abstract interface method is a source- and binary-incompatible change for any CryptoProvider implementation outside the three implementations updated in this PR (custom providers, downstream projects, test providers). Such implementations will fail to compile or throw AbstractMethodError when loaded. It should be a default method (e.g. returning 0 or a documented neutral priority) so existing providers continue to work and can opt in to ordering.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility concern: adding an abstract order() method to CryptoProvider breaks existing implementations that do not implement it.

false_positives.candidate:
Equal order() values silently select an arbitrary provider instead of detecting ambiguity

detectProvider now sorts by order() descending and silently takes element 0, but DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200. If two of those are on the same classpath (the exact situation that previously threw 'Multiple crypto providers loaded'), the winner now depends on ServiceLoader iteration order rather than any intended priority, so an application can silently run with the non-FIPS provider in FIPS mode or vice versa. Ties at the highest order need to remain an error, or the providers need distinct, intentional order values.

ES384/ES512 tests reuse a default-curve key pair and only assert a self round-trip

The constructor generates one EC key pair with no ECGenParameterSpec, i.e. the JCA default curve (normally P-256), and reuses it for ES256, ES384 and ES512. The ES384/ES512 cases therefore never produce real 48- or 66-byte R/S components and only assert asn1->RS->asn1->RS returns the same bytes, which would still pass for DER output that a JDK Signature verifier would reject. Each algorithm should use its matching curve (P-256/P-384/P-521) and the converted DER signature should be verified with Signature.verify (and vice versa) to prove interoperability.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Spawned flusher processes are never killed on hang/crash restart

Processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, whose SpawnProcess class is not an instance of multiprocessing.Process (both derive from BaseProcess). The isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) check at line 254 therefore always fails for the real (non-test) processes, so a hung process is never kill()ed before _create_process_for_shards starts a replacement for the same shards. Two flushers then concurrently call flush_segments/done_flush_segments on the same Redis shards, racing to produce the same segments to buffered-segments (duplicates) or expiring each other's work. The same broken isinstance check at line 346-347 means join() also never terminate()s a hung spawned process. Use multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess (or check for threading.Thread inversely) for these checks.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: processes created with the spawn context are SpawnProcess instances, so the isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process fails on POSIX and prevents hung processes from being killed. Its additional consequences and related check do not change the match.

false_positives.candidate:
--flusher-processes accepts values that crash or are silently ignored

The new click option accepts any int with no validation. Passing a negative value flows through ProcessSpansStrategyFactory into SpanFlusher where max_processes stays negative, num_processes = min(negative, len(shards)) is negative, process_to_shards_map is empty, and 'i % self.num_processes' then raises KeyError/ZeroDivision-style failure while assigning shards, crashing consumer startup. Passing 0 is silently converted by 'max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)' in SpanFlusher.__init__ (line 51) into one process per shard, i.e. the opposite of what the operator requested and a surprising resource jump. Validate the option to be >= 1 (e.g. in the CLI option or SpanFlusher.__init__).

Redis memory backpressure double-counts clusters shared across flusher processes

submit() sums get_memory_info() over one SpansBuffer per flusher process (lines 298-303). Multiple shard buffers that map to the same Redis cluster each report that cluster's memory, so a cluster shared by shards in different processes is counted multiple times in both 'used' and 'available', while a cluster contained in a single process is counted once. Previously a single SpansBuffer covering all shards could deduplicate by cluster. The weighted used/available ratio is therefore skewed toward whichever cluster happens to be split across more processes, causing the hard backpressure (MessageRejected / pausing the consumer) to trigger too early or too late depending on shard-to-process assignment. Deduplicate memory infos by cluster/service before summing.

false_positives.candidate:
Strategy close permanently shuts down the factory-owned shared queue pool

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() calls queue_pool.shutdown(), but ResultsStrategyFactory owns one FixedQueuePool and reuses it for every create_with_partitions() call. Arroyo closes the processing strategy when partitions are revoked/rebalanced and then creates a new strategy for the next assignment; the new strategy reuses a pool whose workers have exited and whose queues have been shut down. Subsequent queue.put() calls raise queue.ShutDown, which submit() then mishandles (see its exception path), so processing after any rebalance is broken and can silently drop work. The pool should be owned/refcounted by the factory, recreated per assignment, or not shut down by the per-assignment strategy.

Graceful shutdown discards queued items instead of draining them

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker.run() checks `while not self.shutdown` before each get(), so a worker that finishes its current item exits even if its queue still contains pending items, despite immediate=False intending a drain. Those unprocessed items are simply abandoned on strategy close (they will only be recovered by Kafka redelivery, if ever), contradicting the graceful-shutdown contract and delaying/losing in-flight processing on every deploy or rebalance.

Failed work items are marked complete and their offsets are committed

OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches every Exception from result_processor, logs it, and then unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in the finally block. The commit loop therefore treats a crashed/failed result as successfully processed and advances the Kafka offset past it, so the message is never redelivered or sent to a DLQ. This contradicts the strategy docstring claim 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and causes permanent data loss for transient processing failures.

Any submit-time exception is swallowed and the offset is marked processed

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() wraps decoding, grouping and queue submission in one try/except; on any exception it logs, then add_offset()+complete_offset() for that message. If grouping_fn raises, the queue is already shut down, or queue.put() fails, the message was never processed yet becomes committable, advancing the offset and dropping the result with no DLQ/InvalidMessage propagation to Arroyo. Only genuinely undecodable/filtered messages should be skipped this way; processing/submission failures must not be marked complete.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the documented guarantee

FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize, and submit() never blocks or raises MessageRejected. The strategy therefore accepts messages from Arroyo as fast as they are polled and accumulates them in memory while a slow group blocks its queue, growing memory (and the OffsetTracker's all_offsets/outstanding sets, which are only pruned up to the blocked offset) without bound and risking max.poll.interval/OOM kills. This contradicts the class docstring claims of 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up'. Bounded queues plus MessageRejected on full are needed.

OffsetTracker state is never reset when partitions are revoked or reassigned

OffsetTracker keeps last_committed/all_offsets/outstanding per Partition for the life of the factory-owned pool, and nothing clears them when Arroyo revokes a partition or reassigns it (possibly to a different committed position, or back to this consumer later at a lower offset after a group reset/rebalance). get_committable_offsets() starts scanning at max(last_committed+1, min_offset), so with a stale last_committed higher than the newly assigned offsets, no offset for that partition can ever be committed again; stale outstanding entries likewise permanently block commits. Tracker state must be (re)initialized from the partitions/offsets passed to create_with_partitions and cleaned up on revocation.

wait_until_empty reports empty while items are still being processed

wait_until_empty()/get_stats() only sum Queue.qsize(), which counts items still waiting in the queue but not the item a worker has already dequeued and is currently processing. As soon as the last item is picked up, total_items becomes 0 and wait_until_empty returns True while processing (and its side effects) are still in flight, so callers/tests/shutdown logic relying on it can proceed or commit-check too early. Use the queue's unfinished_tasks/task_done accounting or an explicit in-flight counter instead of qsize.

The union needs an explicit aggregate such as MAX (or weights 1,0 semantics) to preserve scores.

When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, this pops span_count-1000 members with the smallest end_timestamp_precise scores with no metric, log, or dropped-segment marker. Those spans are permanently lost before flushing, so downstream receives an incomplete segment indistinguishable from a complete one; depending on timestamps this can drop children that ended early while keeping later spans. Segments already buffered at deploy time are regular SETs (created by SADD/SUNIONSTORE) with a 3600s TTL; every one of these commands against them returns WRONGTYPE, failing process_spans/flush until the old keys expire and losing/delaying those in-flight segments. Each algorithm should use its matching curve (P-256/P-384/P-521) and the converted DER signature should be verified with Signature.verify (and vice versa) to prove interoperability.

The weighted used/available ratio is therefore skewed toward whichever cluster happens to be split across more processes, causing the hard backpressure (MessageRejected / pausing the consumer) to trigger too early or too late depending on shard-to-process assignment. true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
